synopsis: A workstation serves an engineer running one simulation at a time, whereas a managed cluster is recommended for thousands of scenarios within four months; HPC is the largest cluster class, intended for scientific calculation [f16210, f16211, f16213]. Samak et al.'s August 2024 GVSETS work used HPC clusters for 128 simulated off-road braking cases because sequential sweeps could not explore the variability space within time constraints, but the booklet treats this as evidence for scaling methodology rather than a prescribed scenario count [f467, f4104, f4105]. The recommended architecture separates commodity-server logic tests, GPU sensor tests, dedicated GPU or HPC soil tests, and local real-time HIL, while accounting for orchestration, database and storage loads [f16220, f16221]. Within the four-month window, throughput matters more than real-time rendering: inexpensive models should screen broadly, reserving expensive models for selected cases, especially compute-intensive terrain simulation [f16219, f6471, f8846]. Illustrative workloads include an aircraft radar calculation taking about 616 ms per angular position on eight nodes with four AMD MI250X GPUs each, and a European virtual-testing study requiring over 800 compute hours plus over 300 hours of manual case selection; these are not compute estimates for the proposed braking system [f4940, f16217, f16218, f10739]. Actual compute expense, cloud or cluster capacity, licensing and labor costs remain unavailable, and on-premises GPU server prices were not found, leaving the architecture recommendation without a substantiated budget [f10739, f8853].
